lesson.title: The Shot That Started a War: Lexington and Concord
lesson.summary: On April 19, 1775, British troops marching to seize colonial weapons clashed with Massachusetts militia at Lexington and Concord, opening the Revolutionary War.
lesson.body:
By the spring of 1775, General Thomas Gage, the royal governor Britain had placed over Massachusetts under the Intolerable Acts, faced a colony that was arming and organizing openly in defiance of his authority. Militia companies known as minutemen, so called because they were expected to be ready to fight on a minute's notice, had been stockpiling muskets, gunpowder, and cannon in towns outside Boston. Gage learned that a significant store of these supplies was being kept in Concord, roughly twenty miles from Boston, and he also hoped his troops might capture Patriot leaders Samuel Adams and John Hancock, who were believed to be staying in the area near Lexington.

On the night of April 18, 1775, Gage sent a force of about seven hundred British regulars marching quietly out of Boston toward Concord. Patriot leaders had anticipated such a move, and riders including Paul Revere and William Dawes set out separately to warn the countryside that British troops were on the move, allowing militia companies to muster ahead of the soldiers' arrival at each town along the route.

At dawn on April 19, the British advance guard reached Lexington, where about seventy militiamen had assembled on the town green under Captain John Parker. Accounts differ on exactly what was said and who fired first, but a shot rang out, followed by a ragged volley from the British troops. Eight Lexington militiamen were killed and several more wounded before the British column reformed and continued on toward Concord.

At Concord, the British searched for the reported weapons cache, much of which colonists had already moved or hidden in the surrounding countryside once warned. A standoff developed at the North Bridge outside town, where a growing force of militia from Concord and surrounding towns confronted the British soldiers guarding the crossing. Gunfire broke out, and this time the colonial militia held their ground and forced the British back, a moment later celebrated as the shot heard round the world.

The British column then began a long, punishing retreat back to Boston, harassed the entire way by militia firing from behind trees, stone walls, and buildings along the road. By the time the exhausted British troops reached safety, reinforced partway by a relief column, they had suffered roughly two hundred fifty casualties compared to about ninety among the colonial forces. Lexington and Concord transformed the political standoff that had been building since the Intolerable Acts and the First Continental Congress into an actual shooting war, and within days thousands of New England militia had surrounded British held Boston, beginning a siege that lasted almost a year.

Dr. Joseph Warren, a Boston physician and Patriot leader, was among those who helped organize the network of riders and lookouts that spread the alarm that night, a system built up over the tense months since the Intolerable Acts had placed Massachusetts under tighter British control. Warren himself would be killed two months later at the Battle of Bunker Hill, one of the first prominent Patriot leaders to die in the war the events of April 19 had begun.
